editorial_title_zh: Photostream Olten #62：琳达·波拉里（Linda Pollari）与奥尔滕施蒂西摄影馆（Photo Stüssi Olten）的人物摄影
editorial_excerpt_zh: 新季开场之际，苏黎世人物摄影师琳达·波拉里（Linda Pollari）将就其最新摄影集《我们之间的时刻》（Der Moment zwischen uns）接受访谈，同时弗里茨·弗朗茨·费格尔（Fritz Franz Vogel）将展示奥尔滕“施蒂西摄影馆”的历史城市风貌，这些影像在奥尔滕早已被遗忘。

article_text:
Zum Start der neuen Saison wird die Zürcher People-Fotografin Linda Pollari zu ihrem neuesten Bildband «Der Moment zwischen uns» interviewt und Fritz Franz Vogel zeigt historische Stadtansichten des «Photohaus Stüssi Olten», die in Olten längst vergessen sind.

Die Zürcher Fotografin Linda Pollari stellt ihren Bildband «Der Moment zwischen uns» vor. Darin versammelt sie Porträts bekannter Persönlichkeiten aus Politik, Kultur, Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft. Ihre Fotografien entstehen aus persönlichen Begegnungen und zeigen Menschen jenseits ihrer öffentlichen Rolle. Zu Beginn führt der Fotograf, Fotohistoriker und Fachpublizist Urs Tillmanns, Autor des Vorworts, kurz in das Buch ein.

Linda Pollari (*1987 in Bern) lebt und arbeitet als Fotografin in Zürich. Nach ihrer Ausbildung in einem Fotofachgeschäft studierte sie Fotografie an der Zürcher Hochschule der Künste (ZHdK) und schloss 2010 ab. Nach mehreren Jahren in der Werbefotografie arbeitet sie heute freischaffend, vor allem in den Bereichen redaktionelle Porträts, Reportagen und Corporate Fotografie. Im Zentrum ihrer Arbeit steht die Begegnung mit Menschen. Pollari interessiert sich weniger für die perfekte Pose als für den Moment, in dem Vertrauen entsteht und Persönlichkeit sichtbar wird. Ihre Porträts entstehen häufig unter engem Zeitdruck und mit möglichst wenig technischer Inszenierung. Ihr Bildband «Der Moment zwischen uns» versammelt Porträts aus rund 16 Jahren Arbeit. Zu den Fotografierten gehören bekannte Persönlichkeiten aus Politik, Kultur, Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft. Die Bilder werden durch kurze Zitate der Porträtierten ergänzt und zeigen nicht nur öffentliche Figuren, sondern auch persönliche Begegnungen und Geschichten hinter den Aufnahmen.

Danach öffnet der Kulturwissenschaftler und Fotohistoriker Fritz Franz Vogel mit historischen Fotografien aus dem Bildband «Photohaus Stüssi Olten» ein Fenster auf Olten und seine Umgebung. Rund 940 Abbildungen dokumentieren das Schaffen einer Fotografenfamilie über drei Generationen hinweg und machen einen bislang weitgehend unbekannten fotografischen Fundus zugänglich. Fritz Franz Vogel (*1957 in Luzern) ist Kulturwissenschaftler, Kunst- und Fotohistoriker, Herausgeber und Kurator. Er lebt und arbeitet in Diessenhofen und beschäftigt sich seit vielen Jahren mit Fotografie, Bildwissenschaft und visueller Kultur.

Mit dem Bildband «Photohaus Stüssi Olten» macht er einen aussergewöhnlichen fotografischen Nachlass wieder zugänglich. Der 240-seitige Band umfasst rund 940 Abbildungen aus sieben Jahrzehnten und drei Generationen einer Fotografenfamilie.Für Olten besonders interessant sind die zahlreichen historischen Fotografien aus der Stadt und der näheren Umgebung: Stadtansichten, Ereignisse, Menschen, Markt-, Verkehrs- und Industrieaufnahmen sowie Bilder der in Olten produzierten Berna-Fahrzeuge. Beim Photostream Olten stehen bewusst diese Fotografien aus Olten und der Region im Mittelpunkt. Eine Woche später wird das Buch auch am Buchfestival Olten vorgestellt. Dort liegt der Schwerpunkt auf der Entstehung des Buches, der Aufarbeitung des Archivs sowie auf Konzeption, Gestaltung und Produktion der Publikation. Zum Abschluss folgt mit dem Photostream Update ein neuer, kurzer Programmpunkt: Moderator André Albrecht zeigt ausgewählte Bilder und vermittelt aktuelle News, Entwicklungen und Tendenzen aus der Welt der Fotografie.

Wann? Sonntag, 25. Oktober 2026, 17:00 Uhr Wo? Im Gebäude «Haus der Museen Olten», Magazin – Bar und Lounge, Konradstrasse 7, CH-4600 Olten Wie viel? Eintritt VVK: CHF 12.00 bei Eventfrog , Abendkasse: CHF 15.00 Infos: Website Photostream Olten

Vorankündigung: Photostream Olten special «s’Füür vo Lieschtel – Herzblut und Asche» , Filmgespräch und Vorführung mit dem Liestaler Filmemacher Stefan Krause Sonntag, 15. November 2026, 17.00 Uhr, Kino Lichtspiel Olten, Klosterplatz 20, 4600 Olten

title_original: Are There Lessons to Be Learned From Gen X?
editorial_title_zh: Are There Lessons to Be Learned From Gen X?
editorial_excerpt_zh: This group exhibition foregrounds Gen X artists that lived the shift from analogue to digital in real time, reality show-to-influencer pipeline, hypercapitalist austerity and trad-fascism
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "这场群展将镜头对准了X世代艺术家，他们实时经历了从模拟向数字的转变、真人秀到网红的产业链、超资本主义紧缩以及传统法西斯主义", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Deste基金会这场群展的策展人马西米亚诺·吉奥尼（Massimiliano Gioni）、卡尔文·王（Calvin Wang）和金台伊（Taeyi Kim）认为，X世代有很多值得学习的地方。“X世代”一词用来描述1960年代中期至1980年之间出生的人，此前加拿大作家道格拉斯·库普兰（Douglas Coupland）于1991年出版了小说《X世代：加速文化的故事》（Generation X: Tales for an Accelerated Culture），书中讲述了一群二十多岁的年轻人反抗美国生活企业化的故事。大卫·什里格利（David Shrigley）的《明天取消了》（Tomorrow is Cancelled，2012）是一块黑色的八角形标牌，上面粗糙地涂写着作品标题，触及了资本主义的死胡同；理查德·林克莱特（Richard Linklater）1990年的电影《懒民》（Slackers）中的一句台词也被梅耶·维斯曼（Meyer Vaisman）的树脂骷髅作品《自画像已故（骷髅）》（Self-Portrait Deceased (Skull) ，1998–2008）的墙面说明文字所引用：“你生产的每一件商品都是你自身死亡的一部分”。为了代替传统的说明，展出的作品均配有摘自X世代书籍、电影和歌曲名言的墙面文字，为展览聚焦的世代以及主要偏向西方的视野增添肌理。在什里格利的作品中，库普兰小说中的一句名言哀叹了“无意义工作的无尽压力”，这句台词预示了X世代活动家大卫·格雷伯（David Graeber）在2013年所描述的“狗屁工作”（此处未提及），即那些贬低生命的毫无意义的工作。不远处，吉莉安·韦英（Gillian Wearing）的C印照片《说你想说的话，不说别人叫你说的话》（Signs that Say What You Want Them to Say and Not Signs that Say What Someone Else Wants You to Say，1992–93）中，一名办公室职员举着写有“我很绝望”字样的牌子，这概括了X世代成长的时代——战后经济繁荣（婴儿潮）时期让位于经济衰退、政治动荡和战争。该作品的墙面文字引用了Run-DMC标志性的1984年曲目《就是这样》（It’s like that），起到了见证记录的作用，描述了创纪录的失业率和“注定要死的人们”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/img307-copy-1230x1862.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Gillian Wearing, Signs That Say What You Want Them to Say and Not Signs That Say What Someone Else Wants You to Say – I’m Desperate , 1992–93, c-print, 133 × 93 × 5 cm. © the artist. Courtesy Deste Foundation, Athens", "credit": "ArtReview", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "考虑到在二十一世纪加剧的历史资本主义的影响——种族主义、民族主义和殖民主义——这一切听起来似曾相识。正如策展陈述所言，这些条件解释了为什么与X世代相关的艺术家成为本次展览的焦点：作为一个群体，他们实时经历了从模拟向数字的转变，宣告了二十四小时新闻循环、真人秀到网红产业链、超资本主义紧缩以及传统法西斯主义的到来。切丽·多尼根（Cheryl Donegan）的低保真录像《头部（第1和第2版）》（HEAD (Versions 1 & 2) ，1993）以一首1992年的另类摇滚谋杀民谣《一个好主意》（A Good Idea）作为配乐，歌中唱到一个男人淹死了一个“似乎并不介意”的女人，画面中艺术家正在饮用从绿色瓶子里喷射出来的牛奶——这提醒人们注意支配女性身体的日常随意的涓滴特权以及为之进行的反抗，正如Sonic Youth在其1990年的曲目《酷东西》（Kool Thing）中呼吁摆脱“白人男性企业压迫”一样，该曲目也出现在其随附的墙面文字中。在其他地方，安德拉·乌尔苏塔（Andra Ursuța）的《世界纪念品外贸》（Commerce Exterieur Mondial Sentimental，2017）是一尊粉红色大理石雕像，原型基于2011年的一张照片，照片中一名罗姆族妇女正等待被驱逐出法国；该作品与暴动女（riot grrrl）凯瑟琳·汉纳（Kathleen Hanna）的一句名言搭配在一起：“当世界只把你当成营销方案中的一个点时，你可以学会这样对待自己和他人。”汤姆·萨克斯（Tom Sachs）的《两架波音767》（Two Boeing 767s，2001）将这一图式推向了更广阔的地缘政治层面，这是一件让人联想起9/11事件的两架飞机的拼贴雕塑；保罗·陈（Paul Chan）的纸本炭笔画《结局》（The End，2012）描绘了萨达姆·侯赛因（Saddam Hussein）被捕前后蓬头垢面的样子，这幅画出现在2012年由陈的出版机构“荒地无限”（Badlands Unlimited）出版的《论民主》（On Democracy）一书的封面上，该书收录了侯赛因在成为伊拉克总统之前发表的三篇演讲，将民主框定为对处于革命中的国家的爱国效忠。伴随陈的画作的节选出自让·鲍德里亚（Jean Baudrillard）1991年的随笔《海湾战争并未发生》，在考虑到美国战争部长皮特·海格塞斯（Pete Hegseth）对士兵外表（更不用说他自己的外表）的锁骨级别关注，以及美国和以色列继续对伊朗和巴勒斯坦进行非法入侵时，这篇节选显得极其具有当代意义：鲍德里亚写道，“这场战争，连同我们在整整一天中看到的对其进行揣测的虚假和假定的战士、将军、专家和电视主持人，正在一面镜子里注视着自己：我够漂亮吗……？”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/DONEGAN-copy-1230x1932.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Cheryl Donegan, Head (Versions 1 & 2) , 1993 (video still). © the artist. article_text:
This group exhibition foregrounds Gen X artists that lived the shift from analogue to digital in real time, reality show-to-influencer pipeline, hypercapitalist austerity and trad-fascism

According to Massimiliano Gioni, Calvin Wang and Taeyi Kim, the curators of this group exhibition at Deste Foundation, there’s much to learn from Generation X. The term came to describe people born between the mid-1960s and 1980, following the publication of Canadian writer Douglas Coupland’s 1991 novel Generation X: Tales for an Accelerated Culture , which follows twenty-somethings rebelling against the corporatisation of American life. David Shrigley’s Tomorrow is Cancelled (2012), a black octagon- shaped sign with the work’s title crudely scrawled on it, taps into that capitalist dead- end, as does one line from Richard Linklater’s 1990 film, Slackers, quoted in a wall text for Self-Portrait Deceased (Skull) (1998–2008), a resin skull by Meyer Vaisman: “Every single commodity you produce is a piece of your own death”. In lieu of descriptions, works come with wall texts featuring quotes from Gen X books, movies and songs in order to give texture to the show’s generational and predominantly Western purview. In Shrigley’s case, a quote from Coupland’s novel laments an ‘endless stress of pointless jobs’, a line presaging the ‘bullshit jobs’ Gen X activist David Graeber described in 2013 (not mentioned here), of work so meaningless it diminishes life. Nearby, Gillian Wearing’s c print of an office worker holding a sign reading ‘I’m desperate’, from Signs that Say What You Want Them to Say and Not Signs that Say What Someone Else Wants You to Say (1992–93), epitomises the era in which Gen X came of age, as postwar boom(er) times gave way to recession, political unrest and war. Wall text for the work quoting Run-DMC’s iconic 1984 track It’s like that functions as a witness account, describing record unemployment and “people born to die”.

It all sounds familiar, given the effects of historical capitalism – racism, nationalism and colonialism – that have intensified in the twenty-first century. These conditions explain why, per the curatorial statement, artists associated with Gen X have been foregrounded in this show, as a group that lived the shift from analogue to digital in real time, heralding the twenty-four-hour news cycle, reality show-to-influencer pipeline, hypercapitalist austerity and trad-fascism. Soundtracked by A Good Idea , a 1992 alt-rock murder ballad about a man who drowns a woman who “didn’t seem to mind”, Cheryl Donegan’s lo-fi video HEAD (Versions 1 & 2) (1993) – showing the artist drinking milk spurting from a green bottle – is a reminder of the casual trickle-down entitlement governing women’s bodies and the generational struggles against it, given Sonic Youth’s call for liberation from “male white corporate oppression” in their 1990 track Kool Thing that appears in its accom- panying wall text. Elsewhere, Andra Ursuța’s Commerce Exterieur Mondial Sentimental (2017) – a pink marble statue based on a 2011 photograph of a Roma woman awaiting deportation from France – is paired with a quote by riot grrrl Kathleen Hanna: ‘When the world only treats you like a dot on a marketing scheme, you can learn to treat yourself and other people like that.’ Visualising that schema on an expanded geopolitical plane is Tom Sachs’s Two Boeing 767s (2001), a bricolage sculpture of two planes invoking 9/11, and Paul Chan’s charcoal-on-paper drawing of an unkempt Saddam Hussein around the time of his capture, The End (2012), which appears on the cover of On Democracy , a book published in 2012 by Chan’s imprint Badlands Unlimited, of three speeches Hussein delivered before becoming Iraq’s president, framing democracy as patriotic allegiance to a state in revolution. The excerpt accompanying Chan’s drawing, from Jean Baudrillard’s 1991 essay ‘The Gulf War Did Not Take Place’, feels sharply contemporary, given US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth’s Clavicular-level interest in his soldiers’ looks, not to mention his own, as the United States and Israel continue their illegal incursions into Iran and Palestine: ‘The war,’ Baudrillard writes, ‘along with the fake and presumptive warriors, generals, experts and television presenters we see speculating about it all through the day, watches itself in a mirror: am I pretty enough…?’

At times, the exhibition feels like a greatest hits of Deste shows, whether at the foundation’s Athens HQ or its Slaughterhouse project space on Hydra, in homage to founder Dakis Joannou’s longstanding curatorial ethos of doing what he wants albeit with an open invitation. Take Chan’s drawings, which followed the artist’s monthlong stay in Baghdad at the turn of 2003, and appeared in Animal Spirits , a 2012 group show at the Slaughterhouse organised, at the height of the Greek economic crisis, around British economist John Maynard Keynes’s description of ‘animal spirits’ shaping economic life. This was among Deste’s most overtly political interventions into the Greek political condition, until its vital Slaughterhouse installation by Nari Ward, Until That Day , opened in June 2026 with a performance featuring Afro-Greek trailblazer MC Yinka, connecting Afro-Greek musical traditions with Rebetiko, a migrant genre. Gestures like these position Deste on the flipside of the wall text for Huma Bhabha’s What Should It Be (2024), a painted and patinated bronze figure resting on a concrete pedestal, which quotes British author Zadie Smith’s 2023 essay ‘The Instrumentalist’, describing the Gen X ‘art monster’ whose talent justifies abuse. ‘What’s wrong with these people is that they are going to die, and for the first time in their lives, they really know that,’ Smith writes. ‘In the curious case of Gen X, we seem to be taking this shocking revelation both personally and collectively, maybe because the end of our time and the end of time itself have become somewhat muddled in our minds. Our backs hurt, the kids don’t like Bach anymore – and the seas are rising!’

Smith questions who’s to blame ‘for this terrible collision of the apocalypse and our own cultural and physical obsolescence’. Is it the millennials or Gen Z? she asks – and it’s here that this show’s argument unravels, given the lack of space to consider the ethical contradictions that shape any group. In a 2024 essay not referenced here, Smith drew a false equivalence between calls for Palestinian solidarity and slogans for mass destruction, echoing talking points designed to obscure the realities of apartheid, ethnic cleansing and genocide in Palestine: a position that ultimately legitimises political indifference as a moral stance. A similar position was expressed by Douglas Gordon – whose slow pan of a couple kissing, titled Monument for X (1998), opens the show – in 2011, when he called the artist boycott of the Biennale of Sydney – over its chairman Luca Belgiorno-Nettis’s role as managing director of longtime biennale sponsor Transfield Holdings, a contractor for Australia’s notorious immigration detention centres – ‘irresponsible’, telling The Guardian , ‘I don’t see any significant change that would have happened if we had all boycotted.’ Seeing as sustained pressure eventually ousted Belgiorno-Nettis and pushed the biennale to cut ties with Transfield, Gordon’s take has aged so badly that it negates this exhibition’s idea that millennials, Gen Z and Gen Alpha could learn from Gen X as they navigate the ethical demands of the moment – especially given the place Gordon’s work has in introducing this exhibition’s entire gambit. Lessons run both ways, after all.

G en X: Tales from the Forgotten Generation at Deste Foundation, Athens 18 June – 26 November

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "荷兰艺术史学家与策展人鲁迪·富克斯在阿姆斯特丹逝世，享年84岁。他的家人于周日向阿姆斯特丹日报《Het Parool》宣布了这一消息。", "links": [{"text": "Rudi Fuchs", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/rudi-fuchs/"}, {"text": "Het Parool", "url": "https://www.parool.nl/amsterdam/rudi-fuchs-84-oud-directeur-van-het-stedelijk-museum-overleden~be884a33/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鲁道夫·赫尔曼·“鲁迪”·富克斯于1942年出生于埃因霍温，1967年至1975年在莱顿大学学习艺术史。1975年，32岁的他被任命为埃因霍温凡阿贝博物馆馆长；当时他是荷兰最年轻的博物馆馆长。这是一段传奇职业生涯的开始，他成为了欧洲顶尖的博物馆馆长之一。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "1982年，富克斯作为德国卡塞尔文献展7展的艺术总监获得了国际认可。富克斯对这一五年一度的展事的诠释标志着对1970年代艺术潮流（如观念艺术、录像和行为艺术）的摒弃——正如《Artforum》当时所指出的那样，富克斯在展览中破例只收录了一件录像作品，即达拉·伯恩baum的《PM Magazine》——转而青睐乔治·巴利茨、基思·哈林以及21岁的让-米歇尔·巴斯奎特等人的绘画和雕塑。尽管它引发了激烈的批评，但它仍将新表现主义推上了1980年代主流艺术运动之一的地位。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在1984年至1991年期间，部分与他担任凡阿贝博物馆馆长的时间重叠，富克斯还兼任都灵里沃利城堡博物馆馆长；1987年，他成为海牙市立博物馆馆长，这一职务一直担任到1993年。同年晚些时候，尽管他离开海牙市立博物馆时留下了超过400万荷兰盾的赤字——他后来公开承认自己“没有管理事务的天赋”——他仍被聘为阿姆斯特丹市立博物馆馆长。", "links": [{"text": "Stedelijk Museum", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/stedelijk-museum/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在市立博物馆，富克斯——以讨厌墙面标签而闻名——以其印象派式的策展而著称，他曾将这种策展比作谱写音乐或创作戏剧。例如，一个名为“对句”的系列将该馆收藏的历史作品与唐纳德·贾德、扬尼斯·库奈利斯和卡雷尔·阿佩尔等当代艺术家的作品进行了配对。他还邀请局外人（包括2000年的贝娅特丽克丝女王）来策划展览。然而，他的任期因财务困难和命运多舛的扩建计划而蒙上阴影，他于2002年卸任馆长职务。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "离开市立博物馆后，富克斯继续作为作家、演讲者和展览策展人保持活跃。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在市立博物馆的Instagram页面上，现任馆长雷恩·沃尔夫斯写道：“作为1982年第7届文献展的艺术总监——这也是唯一一届由荷兰人领导的文献展——[富克斯]崭露头角，成为新绘画的捍卫者；作为海牙市立博物馆的馆长，他改变了蒙德里安被理解的方式；而作为市立博物馆的馆长，他以出人意料的并置和创新的展示方式令观众惊叹……通过他的收藏、展示和出版物，鲁迪为人们理解艺术做出了重大贡献；他所做的一切都在鼓励人们真正去观看。”", "links": [{"text": "Instagram", "url": "https://www.instagram.com/p/De92MzhCP7N/?cplk=MWljOGk3MGdjNnVhNQ%3D%3D"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
Dutch art historian and curator Rudi Fuchs has died at the age of 84 in Amsterdam. His family announced his death on Sunday to the Amsterdam daily newspaper Het Parool .

Born in 1942 in Eindhoven, Rudolf Herman “Rudi” Fuchs studied art history from 1967 to 1975 at Leiden University. In 1975, at the age of 32, he was appointed director of the Van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven; at the time he was the youngest museum director in the Netherlands. It was the beginning of a storied career as one of Europe’s leading museum directors.

In 1982 Fuchs gained international recognition as the artistic director of Documenta 7 in Kassel, Germany. Fuchs’s iteration of the quinquennial exhibition was marked by a rejection of 1970s art trends such as conceptual art, video, and performance—as Artforum noted at the time, Fuchs notably included only one video in the exhibition, Dara Birnbaum’s PM Magazine —in favor of painting and sculpture by the likes of Georg Baselitz, Keith Haring, and a 21-year-old Jean-Michel Basquiat. It opened to fierce criticism even as it launched neo-Expressionism as one of the major art movements of the 1980s.

Between 1984 and 1991, partly in tandem with his directorship of the Van Abbemuseum, Fuchs was also the director of the Castello di Rivoli museum in Turin; in 1987 he became director at the Gemeentemuseum in The Hauge, a position he held until 1993. Later that year, despite having left the Gemeentemuseum with a deficit of over 4 million guilders—he would later publicly admit to “having no talent for administrative affairs”—he was hired as director of the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam.

At the Stedelijk, Fuchs—who famously disliked wall labels—was known for his impressionistic curation, which he likened to composing music or creating a play. A series titled “Couplets,” for example, paired historical works from the museum’s collection with pieces by contemporary artists such as Donald Judd, Jannis Kounellis, and Karel Appel. He also invited outsiders, including Queen Beatrix in 2000, to curate shows. His tenure, however, was marred by financial difficulties and an ill-fated expansion plan, and he stepped down as director in 2002.

After leaving the Stedelijk, Fuchs remained active as a writer, lecturer, and exhibition curator.

On the Stedelijk’s Instagram page, Rein Wolfs, the current director of the museum, wrote, “[A]s artistic director of Documenta 7 in 1982—the only edition ever led by a Dutch person—[Fuchs] emerged as a champion of new painting; as director of the Haags Gemeentemuseum, he transformed the way Mondrian was perceived; and as director of the Stedelijk, he surprised audiences with unexpected juxtapositions and innovative modes of presentation. … Through his acquisitions, presentations, and publications, Rudi made a significant contribution to the understanding of art; everything he did served as an encouragement to really look.”

editorial_title_zh: 档案：让-弗朗索瓦·若索：亲密肖像
editorial_excerpt_zh: 档案 – 2019年10月23日 她是20世纪最重要的艺术人物之一，尽管她始终将自己的情感、性冲动和个人生活融入作品之中，但路易丝·布尔乔亚并不是一开始就容易接近的。你需要证明自己的资历才能获得那张宝贵的通行证。在1994年于她位于布鲁克林的画室进行第一次会面后，摄影师让-弗朗索瓦·若索终于得到了这位艺术家的认可。这次不可思议的会面让让-弗朗索瓦得以在11年的时间里拍摄下珍贵的影像，展现了艺术家在其工作核心处的私密状态。这篇文章“档案：让-弗朗索瓦·若索：亲密肖像”最初发布在《摄影之眼》杂志上。

article_text:
Archives – Octobre 23, 2019

She is one of the major artistic figures of the 20th century, and although she has not ceased to place her emotions, sexual drive and personal life in her works, Louise Bourgeois was not always at first easy to meet. It was necessary to prove your credential to obtain the precious sesame. After a first meeting in 1994 in her studio in Brooklyn, the photographer Jean-Francois Jaussaud is finally dubbed by the artist. This incredible meeting will allow Jean-Francois to make during eleven years rare images that show the artist in her intimacy at the heart of her work.

Tell us about your meeting with Louise Bourgeois?

I met Louise in the winter of 1994, the first meeting was in her office in the Brooklyn workshop a former garment factory at 475 Dean Street. I went through a “questioning” a little strange and fun, an almost administrative questionnaire, date of birth, address, contact details … She noted everything meticulously in a small notebook … Very quickly she realized that I lived near Choisy le Roi, the city where she had spent part of her childhood, she took a great pleasure in making me talk about the city. She asked me to go see the place where her house was at the time and tell her about it at our next meeting. She gave me an appointment in April 1995 for our first photo shoot. One condition: I want to see all the photos and if they do not please me I destroy!

She let only a few people in her privacy, how did you manage to convince her to let you do this work?

April 1995, I arrived at Brooklyn studio, I hired an American assistant to give me a hand because I carried lighting equipment (the studio was divided into spaces bathed in a beautiful natural light and others were just lit by simple light bulbs). My assistant’s name was Robert Miller, I present him, it made Louise laugh a lot, it was also the name of her gallerist! Louise had prepared, specially dressed for her portrait, she was very neat and flirtatious, not in the usual outfit she wore to work in the studio, when she wore layers of worn out clothing, often covered in a blue or gray blouse. First photo, I’m ready, I chose this sculpture “Eyes” two big granite balls that are more like breasts. The sculpture stands in the middle of the studio, Louise is very happy, she is facing the camera, a few words, she turns suddenly, hides her face, suddenly rage, told me that it is not acceptable I attack her, “steal her image”, she goes to take refuge in her office … Stupor, I think that all is finished, I have only to repack my material and return to Paris. A few minutes pass, Louise comes back, with a big smile, she shoves a white cap on her head, placed both hands on the granite blocks: “It’s good, now you can go, I’m protected.”

Two fantastic days in the workshop, I am completely free, I observe, I imbibe, I breathe the place. Louise comes to see me from time to time or it is me who asks for a new portrait, she works, receives, I feel only joy. Two days later, I go to the Chelsea’s little house, 347W 20th Street, I promised to show her everything. B & W contact sheets, color slides, I spread everything on her table, she looks carefully, smiles … “It’s good, you can come back whenever you want”.

You followed her for 11 years, what were the most memorable moments?

Whenever I came to take pictures, I joined her in the morning at 9am we always spent a few moments to discuss before I got to work, she told me about her memories of France and the artists she had known . Beautiful moments of sharing.

Who was she behind the great artist we know?

A woman totally inhabited by her art, there was no difference between her life and her creation. One of her sentences that sums it up perfectly: “Art is a guaranty of sanity”

What seduced the eye of the photographer that you are at the same time of the woman’s and of the artist’s?

In the woman and in the artist the total involvement in her art, she was “Inhabited”. Every time I crossed the threshold of her house I also returned to her, so much was this place incarnated.

How were your photographic sessions?

When I was in New York, I called in the morning before 9am to be sure that she picked up the phone (because her assistant arrived at 9am). Sometimes she was not willing, other times she told me you can come. I arrived then around 10am, she or her assistant opened the door. We then spent a few moments chatting at her desk, then she let me go around the house all day. Joining me from time to time to see me working or for a portrait. I was totally free.

Looking back, did you manage to show her what you perceived from her?

YES !

A regret ?

My last meeting with Louise took place in 2006. I had planned to go to New York at the beginning of June 2010, to go and greet her, she passed on Monday, May 31st …. But, I visit her again very often …

Interview by Carole Schmitz-Chiaroni

LOUISE BOURGEOIS, AN INTIMATE PORTRAIT

Jean-François JAUSSAUD

ストリートファイター ザ・ムービー

劇場公開日： 2026年10月16日

映画館を探す

予告編を見る

映画チケットを U-NEXTでお得にゲット PR

解説・あらすじ

1987年に日本でアーケードゲームとして誕生し、対戦格闘ゲームというジャンルを確立したカプコンの名作シリーズ「ストリートファイター」をハリウッドで実写映画化。 1993年。かつてともに天才格闘家として名を馳せたリュウとケンは兄弟のような存在だったが、ある理由から疎遠になっていた。そんな彼らの前に謎の女性格闘家・春麗が現れ、「ワールドウォリアートーナメント（世界格闘王決定戦）」の招待状を差し出す。リュウとケンは世界最強の猛者であるストリートファイターたちを相手に、ルールもリミットも容赦もない壮絶な戦いに身を投じるが、トーナメントが進むにつれて大会に隠された陰謀が明らかになり、2人が過去に葬り去ったはずの悪夢がよみがえる。 監督は日本生まれアメリカ育ちのキタオ・サクライ。「ブラックアダム」のノア・センティネオがケン、「ブレット・トレイン」のアンドリュー・小路がリュウ、「BAD GENIUS バッド・ジーニアス」のカリーナ・リャンが春麗を演じ、マイク・バイソン役でカーティス・“50セント”・ジャクソン、ベガ役でデビッド・ダストマルチャン、ブランカ役でジェイソン・モモアが共演。日本語吹き替え版では、リュウ役の高橋広樹らゲーム版でおなじみの声優陣が吹き替えを担当。

2026年製作／120分／G／アメリカ・日本合作 原題または英題：Street Fighter 配給：東和ピクチャーズ、東宝 劇場公開日：2026年10月16日

article_text:
自画像 47KMの橋

劇場公開日： 2026年11月11日

解説・あらすじ

中国のドキュメンタリー作家ジャン・モンチーが、父の故郷である湖北省の村を2010年から記録し続ける「自画像 47KM」シリーズの第4作。村の子どもたちとの交流を軸に、村に関わろうとする自身の立ち位置を見つめる。 ジャン・モンチー監督はこの年も、「47KM村」と呼ばれる村に戻ってくる。老人たちへの聞き取りを重ねてきた彼女に子どもたちはすっかり打ち解け、インタビューを手伝ったり、一緒にワークショップを開いたりするようになっていた。中には将来カメラマンになりたいという夢を語る子もいる。だが、ある老人は、農村の子どもが学業で大成したり志を持ったりすることはないのだと言い切る。監督は村の高齢者を支える老人基金を作り、子どもたちとともに支援物資を配って回るのだが……。 ジャン・モンチーは1987年中国湖北省生まれ。中央民族大学でダンスを学び、ダンサー・振付家として活動しながらドキュメンタリーを撮り始めた。2020年には47KM村に家を建てて移り住み、村で暮らしながら制作している。シリーズ全10本を一挙上映する「ジャン・モンチー監督 47KMシリーズ特集上映」（2026年11月7～20日＝ポレポレ東中野）にて日本初上映。

article_text:
Sony Pictures Classics’ John Turturro-starring The Only Living Pickpocket in New York by Noah Segan topped $1.9 million in a major week 2 expansion from six to 1,112 screens. The story of an aging New York pickpocket racing to return a valuable stolen USB drive to a vengeful crime family has an estimated cume of $2.1 million. Rotten Tomatoes’ Certified Fresh at 97% with an 95% audience score, it garnered Turturro a Gotham Award nomination last week and the Golden Eye Award at the Zurich Film Festival in September.

Everest: The Other Side , the National Geographic documentary by Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin debuted to $1 million at 515 locations, with Imax grosses ($825k) accounting for the majority of the total bow. The filmmakers, who have been actively marketing the doc, ascended to the top of a 12-story building on the Sunset strip in West Hollywood, CA Friday evening and successfully rappelled down the side.

Everest Doc And 'Breeder' Anchor Indie Frame With Few New Releases - Specialty Preview

Peter Berg’s WW2 drama The Mosquito Bowl from Netflix, the streamer’s second film in a new regime of box office reporting (for certain projects), opened to $455k on 349 screens. Stars Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgard, Raymond Nicholson and Tom Francis as college football stars plucked from the height of their sports careers and into Marine training and the Pacific theater.

Watch on Deadline

Netflix awards magnet La Bola Negra grossed $418k in week 3 for a cume of $1.2 million.

Limited releases: Mubi’s F atherland by Paweł Pawlikowski starring Hans Zischler and Sandra Hüller grossed $122k at 45 theaters in week 2 for a cume of $250.5k

Neon’s documentary Once Upon A Time In Harlem (100% RT Certified Fresh) grossed $91k in week 3 on 15 screens for a $273k cume. And NAZA , which the distributor recently picked up mid-theatrical run, had a $42k weekend on 80 screens for a $1.9 million cume in week 5 .

Greenwich Entertainment’s Juliette Binoche-starring Queen At Sea , the sophomore feature from Ballast writer/director Lance Hammer opened to $10k at the Angelika Film Center in New York City. Winner of the Silver Bear Jury Prize and the Silver Bear for Best Supporting Performance, shared by Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall, at its Berlin premiere.

New moderate/wide indies: Telugu-language action comedy Aadarsha Kutumbam House No: 4 7 from Shloka Entertainments opened to $1.1 million at 400 locations.

Roadside Attractions’ Sight & Sound Presents: JOSHUA Live! opened to $758k on 1,230 screens.

Christmas at the Kringles from Briarcliff Entertainment debuted at $675k at 1,825 locations.

Samuel Goldwyn Films’ Liam Neeson-starrer The Mongoose by Mark Vaneslow debuted with $480k at 1,014 locations.

Psychological horror Breeder from Independent Film Company/Shudder launched to an estimated gross of $293k for the 3-day weekend for a cume including preview screenings of $566k on 777 screes.

Wide indie holdovers : A24’s hot Elizabeth Holmes doc You Can See Everything took in over $10 million in its third weekend, passing $63 million.

Laika’s animated Wildwood from Fathom Entertainment is tracking towards a $7-$8 million second weekend on its way to surpassing $25 million.

Black Bear’s Wicke r grossed $4.1 million from 2,374 theaters for a cume of $13.3 million. The week two hold (down 28%) is strong as the film broadened its older audience based on critical response and word of mouth and younger audiences continue to recommend the film at higher rates than opening weekend, the distributor said.

Focus Features’ Sense & Sensibility grossed $1.4 million from 1,888 theaters in week 2 for a cume of $16.8 million.

article_text:
Scott Mescudi, the rapper known as Kid Cudi , announced on Instagram that he is working on a biopic about the oft-mythologized New York artist Jean-Michel Basquiat . The film, titled JEAN , will be written and directed by Cudi, who will also star as the titular artist. Cudi shared an image of the first page of a draft of his script, dated August 25, 2026, and said that filming is set to begin in 2027.

In his post, Cudi writes that people have been encouraging him to play Basquiat for years but that “no project actually came to be” so he decided to write it himself. He shared a mock-up of a poster for the film featuring a black and white photograph of himself as Basquiat, stylishly dressed in a suit and tie and smoking a cigarette, with a wig mimicking Basquiat’s trademark free-form dreadlocks. “This isnt the final just a rough,” Cudi writes about the wig. “trust me we gon get it perfect.”

A slideshow of black and white photos of Cudi lounging in what looks like an airy studio space and walking past a wall of graffiti shows him as a rather convincing Basquiat doppelgänger.

Cudi says that the film “will be a love letter to Jean, the 80s and NY city. Jean has inspired me all through out my career, and it will be the biggest honor to tell his story in a way we haven’t seen before.”

JEAN will have plenty of competition. Last fall, a different Basquiat biopic, Samo Lives (named after his graffiti tag, Samo©), began filming in the East Village . Kelvin Harrison Jr. is playing Basquiat and Julius Onah is directing, though updates about the project have been scarce and there is no release date. A film version of Anthony McCarten’s play The Collaboration , about the relationship between Basquiat and Andy Warhol, is also reportedly in the works, though no release date has been set for that either.

Cudi’s film will also presumably need to differentiate itself from the 1996 biopic Basquiat , written and directed by artist Julian Schnabel and starring Jeffrey Wright as Basquiat, and Downtown 81 , a film starring Basquiat as a quasi-fictional artist named Jean, which was shot in 1981 but not released until 2000.

This will be Cudi’s third film as a director. He’s set to direct, write, and star in Doe , about an unhoused man in Hollywood, and is also starring in and directing Wrong Number , a horror film.

In an Instagram story, Cudi says that the time to finally make his Basquiat film is now. “I’m not getting any younger, I’m getting a bit older, and I felt like if I was going to do it, I better do it now. So I’m really f—ing excited, I think you’ll really f—ing love it. Super uplifting, super positive, inspiring. Get ready baby.”

article_text:
Swann Galleries Fall offering of Fine Photographs is set for Thursday, October 15, 2026.

Notable works from the nineteenth century include Francis Frith’s The Pyramids of Dahshoor, from the East , 1857 ($6,000-9,000); and a rare daguerreotype by Felix Jacques Moulin, Two Prodigal Women , 1860s ($7,000-10,000). The auction further features a significant constructivist composition by Alexander Rodchenko, Pushkin Square , 1932 ($20,000-30,000), and a rare portfolio by Todd Webb previously unoffered on the market ($18,000-22,000).

Further highlights include imagery of the American West with Ansel Adams’ Winter Sunrise, Sierra Nevada from Lone Pine, California , 1944, printed April 1978 ($30,000-45,000), and Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico , 1941, printed 1963-70 ($30,000-45,000); and abstraction studies, including ten photographs from the Seaweed Martha’s Vineyard Portfolio , 1943-53, printed 1982, by Aaron Siskind ($7,000-10,000).

The auction also features works associated with the Kamoinge Workshop, including Gordon Parks’ American Gothic , 1942, printed circa 1970 ($6,000-9,000), and Roy DeCarava’s Man Coming Up Subway Stairs , 1952 ($12,000-18,000).

Street photography features Fan Ho, Three Men Walking, Hong Kong , 1962, printed 2006 ($7,000-10,000); and Elliott Erwitt’s oversized Arc de Triomphe, Paris , 1956, printed 2000s ($10,000-15,000). Contemporary highlights feature Peter Hujar’s Keith, N.Y. , 1981 ($10,000-15,000), and Vik Muniz’s Aftermath (Emerson) , from the Children of Brazil project, 1998 ($8,000-12,000). Fashion photography includes images by Richard Avedon, Bruce Weber, Helmut Newton and more.

A selection of press photographs documenting civil rights by Bob Adelman with No Man is an Island, Kelly Ingram Park, Birmingham, Alabama (Civil Rights demonstrators) , 1963, printed 1970s ($4,000-6,000), and Fred McDarrah with George McGovern and Coretta King, Political Campaign , 1972 ($700-1,000), along with examples of vernacular photography, will further enrich the dynamic sale.

Bidding is available through online platforms, absentee, the phone, and live in-person. Live online bidding platforms will be the Swann Galleries website, Invaluable, and LiveAuctioneers.

Swann Auction Galleries is a third-generation family business as well as the world’s largest auction house for works on paper. In the last 80 years, Swann has repeatedly revolutionized the trade with such innovations as the first U.S. auction dedicated to photographs and the world’s only department of African American Art. More than 40 auctions and previews are held annually in Swann Galleries’ two-floor exhibition space in Midtown Manhattan and online worldwide. Visit swanngalleries.com for more information.

Specialist: Alice Le Campion • [email protected] • 212-254-4710 x 66

The complete catalogue can be found here .

title_original: Primetime review – Robert Pattinson’s preening TV host hunts paedophiles but real drama proves harder to target
editorial_title_zh: 《黄金档》影评——罗伯特·帕丁森饰演的爱美电视主持追捕恋童癖，但真正的戏剧张力却更难捕捉
editorial_excerpt_zh: 兰斯·奥本海姆（Lance Oppenheim）关于美国争议性真人秀节目《捕获恋童癖》（To Catch a Predator）的剧情片，对媒体或道德究竟意欲何为显得有些茫然。兰斯·奥本海姆是一位广受赞誉的纪录片导演，他的剧情长片处女作却是一部出奇夸张且略显笨拙的惊悚剧情片……

"但电影真正的戏剧冲突似乎存在于后台办公室的政治斗争和八卦闲聊之中。汉森正试图切断一段婚外情却未能成功，而本德则被一家开出巨额报酬的竞争电视台挖角，对方准备让她制作一档山寨版的汉森节目，并在收视率上彻底压垮汉森和他的节目。有一段时间，一些耐人寻味的阴谋可能性浮现了出来。然而，所有这些都没有走向任何实质结果。实际上，我们只是在走向那个惨烈的大结局——如果恋童癖被当作消遣去追捕和羞辱，这结局本就无可避免；电影平稳推进至危机爆发，此后便认为戏剧冲突已然画上句号，至于汉森是如何改变、妥协或是学到了什么，则完全是个谜。这令人感到失望。", article_text:
L ance Oppenheim is the acclaimed documentary-maker who has made his feature debut with a strangely overwrought and heavy-footed drama-thriller, which for all its elaborate neon-lit atmosphere of noir danger isn’t at all sure what it wants to say about media or morality, or anything else.

The subject is the controversial top-rated US TV reality show To Catch a Predator which ran from 2004 to 2008; that title was evidently taken from the Hitchcock movie To Catch a Thief, which in turn was inspired by the phrase “Set a thief to catch a thief”. In search of prey, the show’s researchers baited paedophiles in online chatrooms posing as children, lured them to “sting houses” where actors played underage teens on the front porch to get the abusers inside, where they can be clearly filmed expressing criminal intentions. But before anything could happen, sonorous host Chris Hansen appeared from nowhere and confronted these cringing abusers – which made for fantastic television. After this the cops made an arrest, and they and the state prosecutor did the heavy lifting of overseeing due process and presumably debating the merits of entrapment in court, although this obvious issue is not raised in the movie.

Robert Pattinson certainly looks and sounds good in the role of the preening, pompous Hansen, gleefully overexcited when his show is promoted to a primetime slot, solemnly congratulating himself on cleaning up America and relishing the bizarrely melodramatic moment each week when he gets in the astonished abuser’s face, sauntering down the stairs with the insouciance of a talk show host. “Big night planned?” Merritt Wever plays Andie Bender, a hardbitten (fictional-composite) female executive in charge of Hansen’s live-ammo theatrics – Bender’s persona inherited from Faye Dunaway in Network – and Skyler Gisondo plays a needy, baby-faced wannabe actor Dan Plumb (another fictional-composite) who is the jailbait decoy that gets to lure the paedo indoors. He is persuaded to take the job by Hansen flatteringly taking him out for a drink, a scene slyly placed before us as a quasi-grooming episode.

Plumb worries that this will not help his acting career long term and of course effectively invites the audience to worry that this is all just playacting anyway, all bread-and-circuses exploitation. The tension ratchets up when everyone realises they have to do something extra to maintain ratings; Hansen becomes obsessed with the rumour that there is a “whale” to be brought to justice in a righteous Texan small town – a high-ranking public figure, not just another sweaty nobody.

But the movie’s own actual drama appears to reside in the backstairs office politics and gossip. Hansen is trying and failing to break off an extra-marital affair and Bender is being headhunted by a rival network prepared to offer huge bucks so she will produce a copycat version of Hansen’s show and crush it and him in the ratings. For a while, some intriguing conspiratorial possibilities present themselves. But none of that leads anywhere. Really we are just heading to the gruesome denouement which surely had to happen if paedophiles were hunted and shamed for sport; the film coasts up to a crisis, after which the drama is deemed to be at an end, although how or if Hansen has changed or conceded or learned anything is a mystery. It’s a disappointment.

article_text:
Some decades look like laboratory accidents: you mix the wrong chemicals, something explodes, and the result gets retroactively labeled a cultural revolution. Britain in the 1990s was one of them. Named fashion director of i-D magazine in 1991 at eighteen, Edward Enninful turned it into the organ of London’s counterculture, amplifying urban voices and avant-gardes alike, before taking the helm of British Vogue for seven years.

He now serves as curator of this retrospective. “Magazines weren’t just documenting culture,” he writes in Tate Etc. , the museum’s own journal, “they were helping to create it.” London at the end of that century bore this out: the magazines were the crucible where everything fused, populated by the same artists, shaped by the same squats, the same freezing studios, the same overheated clubs.

In the pages of The Face, Corinne Day, Juergen Teller and their peers established themselves, in the Tate’s words, “at the forefront of defining a new anti-fashion grunge style.” A pioneer of heroin chic, Corinne Day introduced Kate Moss at fifteen, with a documentary intimacy that dismantled the manufactured glamour of previous decades. Juergen Teller, for his part, gave us Young Pink Kate (1998), the young model caught in the raw light of a disposable flash, as if just woken, irreverent and magnetic.

Nick Knight photographed dancer David Toole, who had his legs amputated in early childhood, for the “Fashion-Able” issue of Dazed & Confused , guest-edited by Alexander McQueen to showcase models with disabilities: a landmark in the history of inclusion. Wolfgang Tillmans closes the chapter with “Concorde Grid” (1997), a series of snapshots of Concorde in flight over London, shot through with “the dual feelings of optimism and anxiety induced by the impending millennium.”

The Young British Artists, meanwhile, had not waited for the millennium to settle their scores. Tracey Emin, Sam Taylor-Johnson and Sarah Lucas “captivated the public with their anarchic spirit and frank work tackling agency, identity and class.” For his zoological vitrines, Damien Hirst submerged dead animals, whole or bisected (sharks, cows, lambs) in formaldehyde-filled tanks, “removing the artist’s hand altogether, the antithesis to low-fi grunge”: death as ready-made. In Chicken Knickers , Sarah Lucas posed a raw plucked chicken against a nude figure wearing a pair of granny underwear, elevating vulgarity into critical weapon while reducing the female body to its crudest terms.

Fashion completes the picture, though to reduce it to that role would be to miss the point. Alexander McQueen, John Galliano and Vivienne Westwood staged shows that were “provocative, dramatic and sometimes nightmarish,” belonging as much, if not more, to performance art as to couture. Hussein Chalayan conceived “design-led clothing inspired by everyday objects,” where exile and identity were literally worn on the body. Ozwald Boateng cut Savile Row to the measure of his Ghanaian heritage, while Mark Leckey, with his video Fiorucci Made Me Hardcore (1999), distilled the quiet melancholy of club nights into art: gestures, all of them refusing any hierarchy between disciplines.

What Tate Britain achieves here carries a gentle irony: opening its doors to a scene that defined itself by its contempt for institutions. By hanging these works beneath its neoclassical ceilings, the museum confers on them a legitimacy they never sought, and might well have disowned. Here they are, canonized against their will.

“The 90s: Art and Fashion” is on view at Tate Britain , London, from October 8, 2026 to February 14, 2027.

article_text:
Members of the Quadracci family have pledged $10 million to establish the Quadracci Pavilion Preservation Endowment Fund, which will support the long-term care and maintenance of one of the museum’s buildings.

Named after donors Betty and Harry Quadracci, who provided $10 million in the 1990s to build it, the Quadracci Pavilion opened in 2001 and is the first building in the United States by Spanish Swiss architect Santiago Calatrava. Housing an exhibition space, reception hall, auditorium, and more, the pavilion is known for its sweeping “wings,” called the Burke Brise Soleil, which look out onto Lake Michigan and are a prominent feature of the city’s skyline.

“Rather than just add something to the existing buildings, I also wanted to add something to the lakefront. I have therefore worked to infuse the building with a certain sensitivity to the culture of the lake–the boats, the sails, and the always-changing landscape,” Calatrava said during the building’s dedication ceremony in 2001.

The donors include the four children of Betty and Harry Quadracci: Joel Quadracci, who is the chairman and CEO of the family company Quad; Kathryn Quadracci, chief executive of QuadMed and president of the Windhover Foundation, the family foundation; Elizabeth Quadracci Harned, president of the Winderful Foundation, which she established in 2023; and H. Richard Quadracci, who passed away this past summer.

In a statement, Joel Quadracci, who is also a trustee of the Milwaukee Art Museum , said, “Our parents believed Milwaukee deserved a building that would make people stop and look up, and the Pavilion has done that every day for 25 years. Building it was the first step. Caring for it is the commitment that makes it last. We want it to be as extraordinary for the next generation, and for every family in this city who thinks of it as theirs, as it was the day it opened.”

The release announcing the gift stated that the newly established endowment fund will “provide annual income to support the long-term care of the Pavilion’s defining architectural features.” It does not seem that there are any immediate structural issues for the building, but that the fund is being established as part of the museum’s yearlong celebration of the opening of the pavilion, which began in August.

“Some buildings change a skyline. Others change the way a city sees itself. The Quadracci Pavilion has done both. It represents the boldness, imagination, and determination that define Milwaukee at its best,” Kathryn Quadracci said in a statement. “This commitment reflects our belief that preserving what makes Milwaukee exceptional is just as important as imagining what comes next.”

The gift is the first major donation secured by director Kim Sajet , the former director of the National Portrait Gallery who joined the Milwaukee Art Museum just over a year ago. “When the Quadracci Pavilion opened, it expressed a belief in what art could make possible for Milwaukee,” Sajet said in a statement. “The Quadracci family’s generosity carries that spirit of civic leadership forward, helping ensure this extraordinary building continues to welcome and inspire generations to come.”

Brandon）35岁，而玛丽安16岁，他还有一个和她同龄的女儿。作为一个现代读者，我发现从投入这段浪漫的角度来看，这是一个很难跨越的障碍，因为他是一个如此明确的长辈形象。我们确实对他的背景故事进行了一些改动，以试图保留其中重要的东西，即他比玛丽安更有经验，见识过更多世面，但去掉了那种令人不适的长辈特质。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "那部电影太惊艳了。有趣的是，他们其实对小说做了不少改动。我想，正因为它已经成为忠实、精彩的时代改编之最高水准，人们几乎忘了它也是一部改编作品，而且他们也做过改动。当你身处这样一个才华横溢的文本的阴影下工作时，这就很有意思了，因为你确实在努力让一切都保持原创，从某种意义上说，这也是一种有益的限制。我们在创作这部电影时，总是在想：“我们该如何把它从人们以前看过的东西中解放出来？”这激发了我们所做的一些增补。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有一个关键场景，我们把它设在了一场派对上，而不是野餐，因为我们当时觉得：“好吧，大家已经看过野餐了。我们怎么能拍出新意呢？”但也有一些是不可避免的。当你把一本400页的书浓缩成两个小时的电影时，某些东西必须被剪掉，而我们剪掉了一些相同的角色和一些相同的剧情节点。我觉得不幸的是，它们居然是一样的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在我们的电影中，爱德华的母亲没有出现，露西·斯蒂ールの妹妹也没有出现，而且爱德华在小屋拜访他们的整段戏在两部电影中都没有出现。你会努力让一切都保持不同。但当你通读原著时，你会觉得：“啊，艾玛·汤普森是对的。那个场景根本没必要，我不会为了追求不同而把它硬塞进去，因为客观上它就是没必要，或者那个角色在里面无所事事。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我在爱德华和埃莉诺的关系上下了很大功夫。我的想法是，在小说中，很大一部分戏剧张力在于她确实不知道他对自己的真实心意，因而纠结万分，心想：“这个男人到底想要什么？”我认为，由于那是一种非常内在的戏剧冲突，它在银幕上其实并不好表现。银幕上真正紧张的，是明知两个人相爱，但他们会不会在一起？问题不在于“他们想不想？”，而在于“命运会不会合谋将他们分开？”这就是我试图构建埃莉诺与爱德华关系的方式：就好像从她抵达伦敦的那一刻起，对他们俩来说，他爱她是显而易见的，问题仅仅在于他们是否被允许将这份爱付诸行动。我只是觉得这样在银幕上呈现效果要好得多，因为它不那么依赖内心状态，而是更多地关乎两个人之间化学反应。他来到巴顿庄园，而她只是说：“你到底想要什么？”这在小说里妙不可言，但在电影里就是不够直观生动。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这样的例子有很多。我得说，这是我写的第一部剧本，但我已经出版了三部小说，自己写了四部。还有一部即将问世，所以我的主要身份还是小说家。我认为从某种意义上说这很有帮助，因为我对这两种媒介各自的优势都非常敏锐。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我有两点要说：第一，在小说中，某个角色的背景故事会让人觉得非常引人入胜，因为无论如何你本来就得自己在脑海中把所有画面都想象出来。所以，当一个角色向你讲述过去发生的事情时，它和其他正在纸面上发生的事情一样具有即时感。但在电影中，由于你目之所见皆是画面，如果你让一个角色去解释某个在银幕外发生的事情，它真的会失去很多冲击力。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在书中，有一些事情，比如布兰登曾提到他与 Willoughby 之间有过一次决斗，但这并没有直接展现在小说的行动中。我们把它搬上了银幕，因为我觉得：“如果你看不到它，在电影里就几乎等于没发生过。”同样地，布兰登有着一段极其复杂的背景故事，在书中他把它讲给埃莉诺听，但我只是觉得，在电影里，一个角色向你讲述某事会失去很多冲击力，除非你觉得讲述这番话的人极为重要。它需要推动银幕上的那种关系向前发展。因此，我们调整了这段对话，让他把这些讲给玛丽安听，而不是埃莉诺，因为这样一来，重点就不再仅仅是背景故事的内容本身，而在于他在玛丽安面前展露脆弱，以及她对他的了解，从而在你正在观看的银幕场景中推进了他们之间的关系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在书中，他们确实都结婚了，但不是在同一时间。在最后一章里，当简·奥斯汀做总结时，她写道，在埃莉诺和爱德华结婚几年后，玛丽安才对布兰登上校日久生情，然后他们才结婚。这就回到了我刚才所说的话，关于当你去创作一部已经被改编过无数次的作品时。简·奥斯汀已经被改编了无数回，不仅仅是这一部作品。你总是在思考：“我该如何向他们展现他们从未见过的内容？”我觉得这很好，因为它促使我们去思考如何能做出一个不同的结局。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我想出了一个在结构上我很喜欢的点子：我们可以展现玛丽安和埃莉诺是如何从彼此身上汲取特质的，因为玛丽安是典型的浪漫主义者，她是那个渴望宏大浪漫人生的人，而埃莉诺一向更加安静。到了最后，埃莉诺得到了那种教科书般的浪漫喜剧式结局——去追逐你一生的爱人，而玛丽安得到的则是一种同样内涵丰富、却节奏更为徐缓平静的归宿。我特别喜欢这种构思，电影的结构呼应了她们性格的互换。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们其实还拍了一场额外的戏，就像是一个尾声。那是几个月后的未来，埃莉诺和爱德华已经结婚了，那是布兰登和玛丽安婚礼的早晨。场景在海滩上，两对情侣在一起闲聚。它最后仍然以这对姐妹的镜头收尾，仿佛故事依然关乎她们的关系，但这是为了向观众表明：“看，他们都很幸福。他们结婚了，成双成对。”这是我们最后拍摄的镜头之一。那是大家最喜欢的拍摄日子之一。天气晴朗美丽。我很想看看这段素材。大家都太高兴了。但后来我们看到了（布兰登）和玛丽安在河边的那场戏，她向他吐露爱意，他们的表演实在太棒了。我们觉得观众不需要另一场戏了，因为从他们俩说话的方式中，你就能看出他们会过得很好，他们之间有那样一条充满同情与爱的河，有那么深的底蕴，而且玛丽安已经长大了。所以这就是为什么我们在埃莉诺奔向爱德华之后就结束了全片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "伟大的艺术就是能够无限改编。我的确认为简·奥斯汀已经达到了那种几乎堪比莎士比亚的地位。她几乎超越了作为文化财产的范畴，以至于我虽然做了一次改编，也并不觉得自己对她拥有任何所有权。我接受会有源源不断的改编，而这只是我的版本，可能已经有人在着手另一个版本了。当角色达到那种文化共鸣和普适性的高度时，它就向任何一代人以及任何与文本产生共鸣的人敞开了大门，让他们把自己的一部分融入其中。我只是觉得，极少数艺术家能达到那种普适性。这是多么大的恩赐，而没有人试图去拍出决定性的版本，这是多么不可思议。每个人都只是在参与这条通过我们都热爱的这部小说连接人类体验的长链。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "至于为什么是她，以及她是如何达到那种不可思议、极其罕见的地位的？我认为这几乎是讽刺主义与浪漫主义的独特结合。我认为简·奥斯汀对社会结构以及人们如何因作为社会人而几乎受到压迫，有着极深的讽刺。但与此同时，她又对爱如何能够成为自主权和真实性的阵地、以及找到一个能真正看懂你的人如何能将你从那些极具压迫性的结构中解放出来，抱有无比浪漫的情怀。我只是觉得这是一个我们永远想要讲述的故事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本采访经过编辑和删节以保证清晰度。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Diana Reid has more to say about “ Sense and Sensibility .”

The screenwriter for Georgia Oakley’s 2026 adaptation starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles grew up watching the 1995 version, from screenwriter and star Emma Thompson. When she was initially pitched the idea to create her own interpretation, she wasn’t sure it could be done because of the success of the earlier adaptation. But she went back to the original text and found the heart of what she felt hadn’t been said on screen before: the love story between the Dashwood sisters.

Reid, who is primarily a novelist, took on her first screenplay from that perspective. In the process of adapting Jane Austen’s 400-plus-page novel into a just-over-two hours film, there were some scenes or characters left on the cutting room floor in order to leave room for the sisters to flourish. Reid was careful to make changes with integrity, not simply because she wanted her version to be different from the 1995 film.

“Sense and Sensibility” is now in theaters. While in Santa Fe, N.M. to be recognized as one of Variety ‘s 2026 Screenwriters to Watch, Reid spoke with Variety about the book-to-screen changes, adapting a classic novel for a modern audience and why she thinks Austen is “almost like Shakespeare.”

I’m a huge fan of the 1995 film. I grew up watching that film. When my producer India [Flint] suggested we try “Sense and Sensibility,” my instinct was that it couldn’t be done because that film had done it perfectly. So, I went away and I reread the book and I rewatched that film, and I had to satisfy myself that I had something to say in the book that I didn’t think had been said on screen before. And I was actually surprised, to be honest, that I did find that in the book.

When I reread the book, I was so struck by the extent to which it’s really a love story between two sisters. I wanted to make sure that, in the film, the spine of the narrative was their relationship. Then, having decided that yes, I would attempt it, it was a process of really paying attention to what resonated with me in the original, the elements of the novel that just almost didn’t require any adaptation at all, that just leap off the page, and making sure that they were really prominent, and then also being honest with myself about the bits that I felt didn’t track as well for a modern audience, and then thinking about how we could massage them while still remaining true to the spirit and the themes of the novel.

From that, I worked out what I wanted to change, and then that gave me a structure, and that was what we pitched to Working Title. That’s the lovely thing about basing it on a really good book. The characters are so fleshed out, so once you’ve pitched it and you have an idea for the structure, when Working Title said yes, I was able to just start at the beginning and then right to the end, and then I edited it.

One thing that really struck both me and my producer was the Willoughby character and the relationship he has with Marianne. It’s actually extraordinary, when you reread the book, how modern that is, and we track it pretty closely, beat for beat. It’s interesting because we have a totally different vocabulary now around those behaviors. But what he does to Marianne is so textbook. He love-bombs her and then ghosts her, and the behaviors are identical to phenomenons that we experience today. I feel like I’ve had those experiences, or friends of mine have had those experiences. That was one that leapt off the page.

Similarly, Marianne’s character in the book, she’s almost ahead of her time. She’s a character that tracks very easily for modern audiences because her impulsivity and her passion is something that we really respect in this day and age. And then maybe there were three things that I felt I needed to massage. One was, there’s a reading of the book where it’s a tale of sensibility yielding to sense, and Marianne, who’s the passionate sister, almost gets crushed by a society that is so oppressive and rigid. By the end, you almost feel like she’s lost some of her wonderful impulsivity and passion. And in this version, I love the idea that maybe there was a way to make it more symbiotic, so that it wasn’t about sensibility yielding; it was more about achieving a balance between the two. I just thought that was such a lovely, elegant structure, if you could set up this antithesis of sense and sensibility, and then have them combine by the end, or have them synthesize. That was another change: Elinor learning from Marianne as well, and then both coming of age at the same time.

And then the final thing was that there are just some features of the original plot that are hard to square with modern morals. The main one being that Colonel Brandon, in the book, is 35 and Marianne is 16, and he has a daughter who’s the same age as her. I find, as a modern reader, that’s a hard hurdle to get over in terms of investing in that romance because he’s such an explicitly paternal figure. We did make some changes to his backstory to try to keep what was important about that, which is that he’s more experienced than Marianne, and he’s seen more of the world, but deprive it of the icky paternal quality.

That film is so phenomenal. It’s funny because they actually do make quite a few changes from the novel. I think because it’s become such a high watermark for a faithful, wonderful period adaptation, people almost forget that it is also an adaptation, and they have made changes. It’s funny when you’re working in the shadow of such a brilliant text because you do try to make everything original, and in some ways that was a helpful constraint. When we were working on the film, we were always thinking, “How can we liberate it from what people have seen before?” That inspired some of the additions we made.

There’s a critical scene that we set at a party instead of a picnic because we were like, “Well, people have already seen the picnic. How can we do it differently?” But then there were some things that were unavoidable. When you condense a 400-page book into a two-hour film, there are certain things that have to be cut, and we’ve cut some of the same characters and some of the same plot beats. And I think that it’s unfortunate that they’re the same.

In our film, Edward’s mother doesn’t appear, and Lucy Steele’s sister doesn’t appear, and there’s a whole sequence where Edward visits them at the cottage, which doesn’t appear in either film. You try to keep it all different. But then when you’re going through the book, you’re like, “Ah, Emma Thompson was right. That scene isn’t necessary, and I’m not going to put it in just for the sake of being different, when it objectively just isn’t necessary, or that character’s not doing anything.”

I did a lot of work on that Edward and Elinor relationship. The way I thought about it was, in the novel, so much of the drama is her genuinely not knowing how he feels about her and her wringing her hands, being like, “What does this man want?” I think because that’s such an internal drama, it actually doesn’t play well on screen. What’s tense on screen is knowing that two people love each other, but that question of will they, won’t they? It’s not, “Do they want to?” It’s, “Will circumstances conspire to keep them apart?” That was how I tried to structure that Elinor-Edward relationship: like it’s clear to both of them, from the moment she gets to London, that he does love her, but it’s just a question of whether they’ll be allowed to act on that love. I just think that plays on screen so much better because it’s less dependent on internal states. It’s more about the alchemy of what’s happening between two people. Him coming to Barton and her just being like, “What do you want?” It’s amazing in a novel, but it’s just not cinematic.

There’s a lot of that. I should say, this is the first screenplay I’ve ever written, but I’ve published three novels, and I’ve written four. Got another one coming out, so I’m primarily a novelist. I think in some ways that was helpful because I’m sensitive to the benefits of both mediums.

The two things I’d say: One is that in a novel, someone’s backstory can feel very compelling because you’re already having to visualize everything for yourself anyway. So, a character telling you a story that’s about something that happened in the past feels just as immediate as anything else that’s happening on the page. But in a film where you’re seeing everything, if you have a character explaining something that happened off-screen, it really loses a lot of potency.

In the book, there were a few things, like there was a duel that Brandon mentions happening with Willoughby, but it’s not in the action of the novel. We put it on screen because I was like, “If you don’t see it, it’s almost like it doesn’t happen,” in a film. Similarly, Brandon has a whole complicated backstory that in the book [that] he relays to Elinor, and I just felt like, in film, a character telling you about something loses a lot of potency unless you feel like the person who’s telling it is really significant. It needs to move the relationship that’s on-screen forward. So, we moved that conversation so that he has it with Marianne instead of Elinor, because then it became not just about the content of the backstory, but then it’s about him being vulnerable with Marianne and her learning about him, and it’s about the progress of that relationship in the scene that you’re watching on screen.

In the book, they do both get married, but not at the same time. In the final chapter, when Austen’s wrapping it all up, she says that a few years after Elinor and Edward get married, then Marianne warms to Colonel Brandon, and then they marry. This goes to what I was saying before, about when you’re writing something that’s already been adapted. Austen has been endlessly adapted, not just this particular text. You are always thinking, “How can I show them something they haven’t seen before?” I think that was good because it pushed us to think about how we could end it differently.

I came up with this idea that I liked structurally: we could show how Marianne and Elinor have taken from each other, because Marianne was the typical romantic, and she was the one who wanted this big romantic life, and Elinor was always the more quiet one. At the end, Elinor gets the textbook rom-com ending of the chase to the love of your life, and what Marianne gets is something that is still really rich, but it’s much slower and calmer. I loved that idea that the structure of the film was mimicking the way that they’ve swapped.

We actually shot an additional scene, which was like a coda. It was months in the future, and Elinor and Edward were already married, and it was the morning of Brandon and Marianne’s wedding day. It was on the beach, and it was the two couples just hanging out. It still finished on a final shot of the sisters, like it was still about their relationship, but it was to show the audience, “See, they’re all happy. They’re married, they’re paired off.” It was one of the last things we shot. It was one of everyone’s favorite days of filming. It was a beautiful, sunny day. I’d love to see the footage. Everyone was so happy. But then we watched that scene of [Brandon] and Marianne by the river, where she sort of confesses her love to him, and their performances were just so amazing. And we just felt like the audience didn’t need another scene because you could tell from the way those two spoke to each other that they were going to be OK, and that there was such a river of compassion and love, and there was so much depth there, and that Marianne had grown up. So that’s why we ended it just after Elinor runs for Edward.

Great art is just endlessly adaptable. I do think that Jane Austen has achieved that status where she’s almost like Shakespeare. It’s almost like she’s moved beyond being cultural property, such that I don’t feel any ownership over her, just because I’ve done one adaptation. I accept that there will be endless adaptations, and this is just my version, and someone’s probably already working on another version. When characters achieve that level of cultural resonance and universality, then it opens it up to any generation and anyone who connects with the text to bring a bit of themselves to it. I just think that so few artists achieve that kind of universality. What a gift, and how incredible that no one’s trying to be definitive. Everyone’s just participating in this long chain of connected human experience with this novel that we all love.

In terms of why her, like, how has she got to that incredible, very rare status? I think it’s almost a unique combination of cynicism and romanticism. I think Jane Austen is so cynical about social structures and the way that people can be almost oppressed by being a social person. But then she’s so romantic about how love can be a site of agency and authenticity, and how finding someone who sees you for who you are can liberate you from those very oppressive structures. I just think that’s a story that we’re always going to want to tell.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

article_text:
“We do high highs and really low lows,” Kate Wyler ( Keri Russell ) tells her husband Hal ( Rufus Sewell ) during another State of the Relationship chat. She’s trying to say she understands their marriage, which has been on the rocks since the Netflix series debuted, is never going to be easy. He’s the Vice President of the United States. She’s the U.S. Ambassador to the United Kingdom. Their date night conversations aren’t about who’s picking the kids up from school or what movie to rent before bed; they’re about who’s going to talk the President ( Allison Janney ) out of instigating World War III and which (extremely attractive) international emissary they should trust with their lives.

“The fights are gonna be spicy,” she says.

Kate wants all this, and so do we. The spice is what keeps “The Diplomat” humming, and the first three seasons may as well have been shot on Arrakis given the plentiful quantities of piquant sand. (Plus, all those interior scenes could’ve been shot anywhere, including another planet.) But back to Kate: She wants Hal so much she’s willing to humble herself before him — to chase him, to prove her devotion, to consider his needs instead of bulldozing past them to enact her own agenda.

On the one hand, the plan makes sense: Kate cheated on Hal and broke his heart. Now, she wants to fix it. But as healthy as that might be for their marriage, it’s a disaster for “ The Diplomat .”

Debora Cahn’s political drama about political relationships — and relationship politics — thrives on the layered, overlapping tensions between Kate’s love for her job and her love for her spouse. Each one is high-stakes. Each one hangs by a thread. And each one requires Kate to put all of herself on the line — to save her marriage and save the world.

So when she’s suddenly holding back in deference to her husband’s position, the series loses its foundational source of suspense. Seeing the Wylers work as a team may be a nice, cozy idea, but it neuters the drama, shifting all the weight onto political maneuverings that are simultaneously too close to reality to offer effective escapism and too far from reality to provide cathartic insight. And seeing them square off against another power couple — even one played by Bradley Whitford and recent Emmy winner Allison Janney — isn’t spicy. It’s easy and one-sided, whereas Kate and Hal’s old brouhahas were so emotionally and politically byzantine part of the thrill simply came from keeping up.

Speaking of easy, Season 4 kicks off with a hackneyed “twist” that speaks to the fumes the series appears to be running on (mild spoilers for Episode 1 ahead): President Grace Penn is shot! Fallout from her clandestine theft of a Russian super-nuke (at the end of Season 3) is put on hold while surgeons dig a bullet out of Grace’s guts — not that we see the surgery, or even much of the shooting. That would be a tad too visceral for Cahn’s talky drama, and while the gunshot itself is well-staged by director Alex Graves, what is technically a pivotal moment (in the diegetic history of “The Diplomat,” as well as the overall season) soon feels like little more than a marker in time, when an already hostile president is given extra ammunition to lean into her aggressive tendencies.

The sea change expands the existing divide between the diplomat and her administration (Kate always thought President Penn was dangerous, if not unfit for office), leading to a lot of backroom discussions about how to handle an antagonistic, unreasonable Commander in Chief — and golly gee, what would that be like? “The Diplomat” has always existed in its own imaginary political bubble, which works well enough when its global crises are held at the same theatrical level as its romantic melodrama. But in Season 4, the balance is off, and the fictional president’s parallels to our real-life war-starting, ally-betraying POTUS only make the former’s plight feel that much more trivial.

To be frank, I would love to live in a world with the problems brought on by President Penn rather than the ones produced by President Trump. I’d be just as happy not to think about President Trump at all while watching what’s always been, even at its best, a slick and silly Netflix drama . But without the usual marriage drama, the political drama edges too close to a polite simulation of what’s really going on in Washington, which spoils any hope of suspending disbelief.

Cahn and co. do try to replace the tension lost in Kate and Hal’s renewed commitment. President Penn and her husband Todd (Whitford) get to throw down now and then, as a husband who already feels emasculated has to sit and watch his wife recede into bitter militance. On the other end of the spectrum, there’s Stuart (Ato Essandoh) and Eidra (Ali Ahn), a young couple edging ever closer toward long-term commitment. Their romantic gestures are sweet, just as their tender setbacks prove stinging, but the relationship triptych — the young, kinda naive couple, the middle-aged, mid-life-crisis couple, and the senior, over-it couple — doesn’t go deep enough to replace the juice of Kate and Hal’s turbulent connection. (They were just right !)

Our star couple still fights (and Russell, Sewell, and particularly Whitford contribute strong performances while quarrelling), but after, in prior seasons, tumbling down from the “high highs” of a passionate marriage to an informal separation and assumed divorce, the Wylers’ new alliance (formalized during an impromptu vow renewal in Episode 1) proves too stable. He’s too much of an open book (remember when Hal was a wild card? that was fun!), and she’s too much of a glorified assistant (writing his speeches, delivering his messages, secretly holding up cue cards during Zoom calls — woof). Kate is no one’s lackey, and watching her spend the better part of a season pretending she could be is unconvincing. And it just feels wrong.

“The Diplomat’s” core strength was in its central relationship. Season 4 dilutes that power across three couples, one of whom occupies the highest office in America. But a lofty title is no substitute for rewarding work, just as a respectable union built on lies is no better than an honest partnership contingent on one unbreakable vow:

The fights have got to be spicy.

Grade: C

“The Diplomat” Season 4 premieres Thursday, October 15 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.
excerpt_original: From a desperate opening twist to a maddeningly subservient Kate Wyler ( Keri Russell ), the latest season of Debora Cahn's elevated chamber drama inadvertently dilutes its power by chasing more.

editorial_title_zh: 米兰将拍卖一件乔治·瓦萨里（Giorgio Vasari）的画作
editorial_excerpt_zh: Il Ponte拍卖行即将拍售《基督下葬》（Trasporto di Cristo al Sepolcro），这是一件时隔半个多世纪后重返市场的巨幅木板画。估价为：200.000-250.000欧元。本文《米兰将拍卖一件乔治·瓦萨里（Giorgio Vasari）的画作》源自exibart.com。

Arredi e Dipinti antichi）上的主角。“这一发现对该艺术家的研究具有重要意义，它使我们能够确认为其亲笔真迹，并将其创作时间定在1540年至1545年之间，”该拍卖行的公告中如是声明。估价是多少？在200.000至250.000欧元之间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对这块木板画的创作技法给予了特别关注。这幅画以一种格外充满活力的手法脱颖而出（拍卖行将其形容为“不同于该艺术家木质载体作品通常的精细收尾”）。人物是通过快速而果断的笔触构建的，在某些地方可以隐约看到底层的底子，这种效果让人联想起湿壁画的清新感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
Un’opera di Giorgio Vasari torna sul mercato dopo oltre mezzo secolo. È il Trasporto di Cristo al Sepolcro , una monumentale tavola – 159×185 cm! – protagonista dell’Asta di Arredi e Dipinti antichi in programma a Milano, dal 28 al 30 ottobre. «Il ritrovamento, di significativa rilevanza per gli studi sull’artista, ha consentito di confermarne la piena autografia e di collocarne l’esecuzione tra il 1540 e il 1545», dichiara un comunicato della maison. La stima? Una cifra compresa tra 200.000 e 250.000 euro.

Attenzione speciale alla tecnica esecutiva della tavola. La pittura si distingue per un approccio particolarmente energico («insolito rispetto alla consueta finitura delle opere su supporto ligneo dell’artista», lo definisce la casa). Le figure sono costruite attraverso pennellate rapide e incisive, che in alcuni punti lasciano intravedere la preparazione sottostante, con un effetto che richiama la freschezza della pittura ad affresco.

Dalla Maddalena inginocchiata ai piedi di Cristo alle profonde pieghe della tunica gialla del personaggio barbato sulla destra, la superficie pittorica rivela una notevole sicurezza esecutiva. Sono dettagli che contribuiscono a fare della riscoperta un’occasione per approfondire la varietà delle soluzioni tecniche sperimentate dall’artista nella prima metà del Cinquecento.

Non solo Vasari: gli altri highlights in asta, da Fra Galgario agli argenti rari

Accanto al Vasari, la selezione di dipinti antichi all’asta comprende opere di particolare interesse. Tra queste, il Ritratto di un conte Secco Suardo di Vittore Ghislandi, detto Fra Galgario, proposto con una stima di 40.000-60.000 euro, e la Veduta del Campo Vaccino di Antonio Joli, in catalogo per 90.000-100.000 euro.

Non solo dipinti antichi. La vendita comprende anche arredi e oggetti da collezione dalle caratteristiche singolari. Tra questi, un tavolo circolare ottocentesco con quattro sostegni scolpiti a forma di levrieri, proveniente dalla collezione della Principessa Borghese di Roma, stimato 4500-5000 euro, e un micromosaico ottocentesco di Georg Ferdinand Wekler raffigurante la residenza imperiale di Elagin, presso San Pietroburgo, con una stima di 6000-8000 euro.

Il calendario prosegue il 30 ottobre con l’Asta di Argenti importanti . Tra gli highlights della categoria, una coppia di alzate in argento cesellato e traforato firmate Garrards, Panton Street, London, riconducibili alla produzione di Robert Garrard II e stimate 30.000-35.000 euro. E ancora un trofeo equestre in oro 18 carati, assegnato al vincitore della Coppa Duca d’Aosta all’Ippodromo di Mirafiori, a Torino, il 1° luglio 1928. Oggi, da Il Ponte Casa d’Aste, potrebbe passare di mano per 20.000-22.000 euro.
excerpt_original: Il Ponte mette in vendita il "Trasporto di Cristo al Sepolcro", una tavola monumentale che torna sul mercato dopo oltre mezzo secolo. La stima: € 200.000-250.000 L'articolo C’è un dipinto di Giorgio Vasari all’asta a Milano proviene da exibart.com .

article_text:
Cine

Sacrificio: los elegidos – Crítica de la película

Lalo Ortega

Aunque con sólidas actuaciones del elenco liderado por Anya Taylor-Joy, ‘Sacrificio: los elegidos’ no trasciende sus tópicos de “Eat the Rich”.

Ya hemos estado aquí –y con bastante frecuencia en los últimos años–: historias en las que los frívolos, egocéntricos y desconsiderados millonarios, celebridades y complacientes artistas se vuelven víctimas de la venganza por sus actos en contra de –o apatía hacia– los oprimidos o el planeta Tierra. Vamos, que incluso Anya Taylor-Joy y Chris Evans han estado en algunas . Ambas excelentes, por cierto, lo que sólo exalta la poca gracia con la que Sacrificio: los elegidos ( Sacrifice ), de Romain Gavras, se une a dicho canon.

Difícil no sentir su premisa como un lugar común: la película nos sitúa en una gala benéfica, en donde CEOs billonarios y celebridades variopintas, ataviadas en trajes y vestidos de diseñador, intercambian ideas y discursos vacíos sobre salvar el planeta. Entre ellos está Mike Tyler (Evans), una estrella de cine intentando recuperarse de una funa; Ben Bracken (Vincent Cassel), el techbro más rico del planeta; su esposa estrella de pop y productora, Gloria (Salma Hayek); y la artista Katie (Ambika Mod).

Sin embargo, un culto armado, liderado por Joan (Taylor-Joy), irrumpe en la gala con una declaración radical: un volcán hará erupción en tres días y acabará con la vida en la Tierra… a menos que tres personas sean sacrificadas en su lava. Al ser secuestrado por el culto junto con Ben y Katie, Mike es arrojado al rol más heroico de su carrera en la vida real. Si tan solo pudiese capitalizarlo…

Desarrollándose como una suerte de road movie satírica en camino hacia el volcán, la película Sacrificio se construye sobre dicotomías: la del mundo natural contra la explotación industrial; la de la razón y la ciencia contra el pensamiento mágico; la de la colectividad contra el individualismo; la del querer buscar el beneficio colectivo contra sólo pretenderlo ante la cámara.

La cuestión es que, aunque el guion de Will Arbery ( Succession ) introduce esos temas a través de sus personajes –y con sólidas actuaciones del elenco–, en su mayoría no son llevados más allá del arquetipo, algunos incluso quedando en la caricatura. La trama, eventualmente, nos revelará algo del pasado de Joan, por qué cree en lo que cree y si sus métodos podrían o no ser legítimos; y por lo menos Mike sigue una cierta estructura del “viaje del héroe” que plantea su introspección y jugando con la ambigüedad al borde de su abismo personal: ¿tendrá una epifanía, o sólo sacará provecho de la situación?

Sin embargo, más allá de eso, Sacrificio permanece en la sátira superficial y en un absurdismo que oscila de lo evidente –como que la ética y la acumulación extrema de riqueza no se llevan– a, en contadas ocasiones, lo punzante e incómodo –como que el compromiso con la subversión implica sacrificios personales que no todos están dispuestos a cumplir.

Pero quedarse en ese nivel es, paradójicamente, tan efectivo como ser una estrella de Hollywood que va a tomarse fotos en una gala benéfica con la élite mundial. ¿No podemos hacer o decir nada más que burlarnos de la idiotez billonaria, llegados a este punto?

Lalo Ortega Este no es el droide que estás buscando. Crítico y periodista de cine, edita el blog de Film Club Café y también publica en La Estatuilla. Anteriormente, fue editor en jefe de Filmelier en México y Brasil, y editor web para EMPIRE en español.

而且在过去的几年里非常频繁 - 故事,在那里热情的,自我中心和无视的百万富翁,名人和令人满意的艺术家成为他们的行为的报复的受害者 - 或对 - 压迫或地球的无情。罗马因·加布拉斯(Romein Gavras)的《牺牲》(Sacrifice)》将与这条通道联系起来。", "links": [{"text": "han estado en algunas", "url": "https://cinepremiere.com.mx/el-menu-critica-de-la-pelicula.html"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "很难不像一个常见的地方那样感觉到他的预言:这部电影将我们置于一个有益的聚会,在那里数十亿首席执行官和多人名人,穿着设计师的衣服和衣服,交换了关于拯救地球的空虚想法和演讲。艺术家卡蒂(Ambika Mod)", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而,由Joan(Taylor-Joy)领导的武装崇拜,在加拉中陷入了激进的声明:火山将在三天内爆发,并将终止地球上的生命......除非三个人在他的拉瓦中被牺牲。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.cinepremiere.com.mx/uploads/2026/10/pelicula-sacrificio-estreno-chris-evans-900x512.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Cine PREMIERE", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为一種在火山之路的撒蒂里性路電影,這部電影《犧牲》是基於數字的:自然世界對工業利用的,理性和科學對魔法思維的,集體性對個體主義的,想要尋找集體利益的,而只是在房間面前尋求利益的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "问题在于,虽然Will Arbery的剧本( Succession)通过他的角色 - 并与坚实的表演 - 引入这些主题,但他们大多不是超越档案,有些甚至留在漫画中。迷信和在你的个人荒野边缘的双重性游戏:你会有一个癫痫,或者你只会从情况中获益?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而,超越这一点,牺牲仍然存在于表面性撒旦和荒谬的荒谬之中,从显而易见的 - 如道德和极端财富积累不被带到 - 有时是令人震惊和不舒服的 - 如承诺屈辱意味着个人牺牲,而不是每个人都愿意履行。", "links": [{"text": "Sacrificio", "url": "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacrifice_(2025_film)"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但是,在这个层次上留下来,悖论地说,就像是好莱坞明星在与世界精英有益的聚会上拍摄照片一样有效。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.cinepremiere.com.mx/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/CP-favicon-512.jpg'", "alt": "作者", "caption": "", "credit": "Cine PREMIERE", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Lalo Ortega Este 不是你正在寻找的 droide. 评论家和电影记者,编辑了电影俱乐部咖啡馆的博客,并在La Statuilla上发布。", "links": [{"text": "Lalo Ortega", "url": "https://cinepremiere.com.mx/author/lortega"}], "translated": true}]
